claim: T. gondii CPSF1 displays nuclear staining by immunofluorescence in human primary fibroblasts infected with parasites expressing an HA-Flag-tagged copy of CPSF1.
source: A representative image of the nuclear staining CPSF1 (red) in human primary fibroblasts (HFFs) infected with parasites expressing an HA–Flag-tagged copy of CPSF1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the figure legend and supported by the immunofluorescence image in Figure 1A showing nuclear localization.

claim: MS-based proteomic analysis of CPSF1-Flag elution identified many of the CPSF complex subunits.
source: MS-based proteomic analysis of the CPSF1-Flag elution identified many of the CPSF complex subunits.
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fip1 was detected in sub-stoichiometric quantities in higher molecular weight band extractions but no band at its predicted size was cut-out for analysis.
source: Fip1 was detected in sub-stoichiometric quantities in higher molecular weight band extractions but no band at its predicted size was cut-out for analysis.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B.

claim: CPSF4 in T. gondii harbors a YTH domain in addition to conserved zinc fingers, an architecture shared with plants.
source: Domain architectures representation of CPSF4 homologues. Hs Homo sapiens, Dm Drosophila melanogaster, Sc Saccharomyces cerevisiae, At Arabidopsis thaliana, Cv Chromera velia, Tg Toxoplasma gondii, Cp Cryptosporidium parvum. CPSF4 in T. gondii is encoded by TGME49_201200.
evidence: The domain architecture diagram in Figure 1D shows the presence of both zinc fingers and YTH domain in T. gondii CPSF4.

claim: The metazoan and fungi counterparts of CPSF4 display five distinctive and evolutionary-conserved CCCH-type zinc fingers, in addition to a zinc knuckle, but none of them present the YTH domain within the same protein.
source: In comparison, the metazoan and fungi counterparts display five distinctive and evolutionary-conserved CCCH-type zinc fingers, in addition to a zinc knuckle, but none of them present the YTH domain within the same protein (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by the domain architecture comparison in Figure 1D.

claim: The unique protein arrangement bringing together a C-terminal YTH domain with N-terminal CCCH zinc finger motifs has been detected in apicomplexans and is also conserved in higher plants.
source: A unique protein arrangement bringing together a C-terminal YTH domain with N-terminal CCCH zinc finger motifs has been detected in apicomplexans, but not exclusively, as it seems to also be conserved in higher plants (Stevens et al., 2018).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Stevens et al., 2018.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana CPSF30 gene produces two isoforms: CPSF30L (with YTH domain) and CPSF30S (without YTH domain).
source: This architecture is detected on one of two isoforms of the CPSF homolog (CPSF30 gene At1g30460) in Arabidopsis thaliana, namely the CPSF30L, while the short version CPSF30S is one that lacks the YTH domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; Chakrabarti and Hunt, 2015; Delaney et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with citations to multiple supporting studies.

claim: The alternative splicing and polyadenylation events that form the double plant isoforms of CPSF30 are not seen in the T. gondii homolog which is expressed in a constitutive manner throughout the parasite life cycle.
source: The alternative splicing and polyadenylation events that form these double plant isoforms, is not seen in the T. gondii homolog which is expressed in a constitutive manner throughout the parasite life cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and is consistently predicted as a 62 kDa protein.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP display nuclear localization in T. gondii.
source: IFA showing the nuclear localization of METTL3, METTL14 and WTAP (red), using human primary fibroblasts (HFFs) infected with the corresponding parasites harboring endogenously HA-FLAG-tagged proteins.
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend and supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2A showing nuclear staining.

claim: WTAP displays both nuclear and cytoplasmic staining, hinting at the ability of this protein to shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
source: In addition to its nuclear staining, the WTAP protein displayed a diffused staining throughout the cytoplasm, hinting at the ability of this protein to shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by the immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: METTL3 and METTL14 form an intact RNA methyltransferase core complex with an apparent molecular weight of 400-500 kDa by size exclusion chromatography.
source: These partnerships were subsequently resolved by mass spectrometry-based proteomics which identified METTL3 and METTL14 as an intact RNA methyltransferase core complex (Figure 2C) with an apparent molecular weight of 400–500 kDa by size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry and gel filtration data in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: WTAP was found in the METTL3 pull-down in significant quantities despite stringent washing conditions.
source: Although METTL14 was not detected in the eluates of WTAP and vice versa, WTAP was found in the METTL3 pull-down in significant quantities despite the stringent washing conditions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Treatment of METTL3-mAID-HA parasites with IAA triggered a highly specific and near-complete clearance of the METTL3 protein after 24 hr.
source: Treatment of the edited parasites with indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) triggered a highly specific and near-complete clearance of the pool of METTL3–mAID–HA protein after 24 hr (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The m6A mark is detected mostly within the cytoplasm by immunofluorescence staining in tachyzoites.
source: The m6A mark is detected mostly within the cytoplasm by immunofluorescence staining in tachyzoites (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C.

claim: METTL3 knockdown triggers a significant reduction in m6A levels as early as 12 hr after IAA treatment, with a more dramatic decrease after 24 hr.
source: Consistent with its role as a catalytically active subunit, METTL3 knockdown triggers a significant reduction in m6A levels as early as 12 hr after IAA treatment, with a more dramatic decrease after 24 hr (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence and ELISA data in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: CRISPR-based transitory genetic inactivation of METTL3 resulted in a significant drop in m6A levels.
source: It should be noted that along with this post-translational loss of METTL3, a CRISPR-based transitory genetic inactivation of this protein resulted in a similarly significant drop in the m6A levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: T. gondii CPSF4-YTH domain binds to m6A-modified RNA with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 5.05 ± 0.44 μM.
source: IsoThermal Calorimetry (ITC) titrations obtained from recombinant TgCPSF4YTH (B) or AtCPSF4YTH (C) against unmodified (left panel) or m6A modified seven mer RNA (right panel).
evidence: The Kd value is shown in the ITC data in Figure 4B.

claim: T. gondii CPSF4-YTH domain shows almost no binding affinity to unmodified RNA.
source: As measured, binding towards the RNA substrate has a relatively high dissociation constant (Kd) but is entirely dependent on the presence of an m6A modification as almost no binding affinity is measured in the un-modified RNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by ITC data in Figure 4B showing no binding to unmodified RNA.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana CPSF30 YTH domain binds to m6A-modified RNA with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 0.33 ± 0.03 μM.
source: IsoThermal Calorimetry (ITC) titrations obtained from recombinant TgCPSF4YTH (B) or AtCPSF4YTH (C) against unmodified (left panel) or m6A modified seven mer RNA (right panel).
evidence: The Kd value is shown in the ITC data in Figure 4C.

claim: The crystal structure of T. gondii CPSF4-YTH domain in complex with m6A-modified RNA was determined at 1.45 Å resolution.
source: TgCPSF4-YTH (aa 434–598), as used in the ITC experiments generated distinct crystal forms: Apo, m6A bound and m6A modified 7-mer RNA bound (Supplementary file 2) which all diffracted to high resolutions (up to 1.45 Å for the RNA bound form), sometimes using fully automated upstream crystal harvesting (using the EMBL crystal direct technology) and automated crystal diffraction (using MASSIF-1 at the ESRF).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and the resolution is provided.

claim: The CPSF4 YTH domain folds into a well-structured domain featuring six alpha helices (α1–6) and five beta sheets (β1–5).
source: Overall, the CPSF4 YTH domain folds into a well-structured domain (Figure 5A) featuring six alpha helices (α1–6) and five beta sheets (β1–5).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The m6A-binding site in CPSF4-YTH involves residues in, or close to, helices α1/α2/α3 and beta sheet 1.
source: The m6A-binding site involves residues in, or close to, helices α1/ α2/ α3 and beta sheet 1 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by the crystal structure in Figure 5A.

claim: The binding of m6A does not induce important conformational changes within the CPSF4-YTH protein.
source: The binding of m6A favors crystal growth in P1 symmetry instead of a P41212 symmetry, however, the binding event does not induce important conformational changes within the protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), the N-terminal residues (ranging from 437 to 446) fold as random coils on opposite sides, most likely as a consequence of crystal packing.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by structural comparison in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: T. gondii CPSF4-YTH and human YTHDC1 share a sequence identity of 38%.
source: When comparing the CPSF4 YTH domain with its closest homologue structure (human YTHDC1), the overall general conservation of the domain is observed (Figure 5B) with both sharing a sequence identity of 38% and having most of their secondary structure features conserved (Figure 5C), apart from α3 and β1 which are unique secondary structures to CPSF4 YTH.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by structural comparison in Figure 5B.

claim: The aromatic cage recognizing m6A in CPSF4-YTH displays a notable difference in the region between residues 519 and 526 compared to human YTHDC1, with the absence of a methionine residue (M434 in YTHDC1) and the presence of an additional valine (V522).
source: Although strongly conserved, the aromatic cage recognizing the m6A displays a notable difference in the region between residues 519 and 526 (res 428–439 in the human YTHDC1) with the absence of a methionine residue (M434 in YTHDC1) and the presence of an additional valine (V522).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text describing structural differences.

claim: The depletion of CPSF4 was accompanied by an apparent transcriptional readthrough that went beyond the annotated 3'end sequence of a certain gene to breach into the adjacent one, generating very long transcripts.
source: At many loci, the depletion of CPSF4 was accompanied by an apparent transcriptional readthrough that went beyond the annotated 3'end sequence of a certain gene to breach into the adjacent one, and that generated very long transcripts (top of Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nanopore long-read Direct RNA Sequencing data indicate that the initial 3'end polyadenylation site has been overrun following CPSF4 depletion, and that the process has shifted to employ an alternative PAS within the downstream gene.
source: Could this defect in the transcription termination be caused by an overrun of the gene's proximal polyadenylation signal (PAS)? Nanopore long-read Direct RNA Sequencing (DRS) data argue in favor of this suggestion, and point to an alternative 3'end processing that is occurring using the downstream PAS of the adjacent gene (bottom of Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by nanopore DRS data in Figure 7E.

claim: The depletion of METTL3 phenocopies that of CPSF4 in generating transcriptional readthrough chimeric RNAs.
source: Nanopore DRS analysis revealed recurrent events of transcription termination defects in METTL3-depleted cells when compared to untreated cells, at loci that exhibited similar patterns in the context of CPSF4 being depleted (Figure 7E, Figure 8 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by nanopore DRS data comparing METTL3 and CPSF4 knockdowns.

claim: Most of the observed readthrough events within the METTL3 KD are also found in the CPSF4 KD.
source: Overall, most of the observed readthrough event within the METTL3 KD are also found in the CPSF4 KD (Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by comparative analysis in Figure 8B.

claim: CPSF4 has a higher number of readthrough events than METTL3 because of its central role to recruit the CPSF complex which can be independent of m6A.
source: CPSF4 also has a higher number of readthrough events because of its central role to recruit the CPSF complex which can be independent of m6A (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 8C.

claim: The formation of RNA chimeras following the depletion of CPSF4 and METTL3 occurred globally over all chromosomes.
source: We detected and assessed the average distribution of readthrough transcripts at a genome-wide level, by using ChimerID scripts (Parker et al., 2020), and concluded that the formation of RNA chimeras following the depletion of CPSF4 and METTL3 occurred globally over all chromosomes (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by genome-wide analysis in Figure 8A.

claim: Nanopore DRS data from Arabidopsis thaliana confirmed the existence of single full-length chimeric transcripts in fip37L and cpsf30-3 mutants.
source: The nanopore DRS data generated from these samples allowed the confirmation of the existence of single full-length chimeric transcripts in the mutants, as revealed by an increase in the number of reads of a set of genes, when compared to their repressed state in the WT samples (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by nanopore DRS data in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: In Arabidopsis mutants, the mutation-specific increase in chimeric transcripts was caused by a readthrough of an upstream gene that did not terminate and read into the adjacent gene, terminating at the PAS of the latter instead.
source: This mutation-specific increase was evidently caused by a readthrough of an upstream gene, the transcription of which did not terminate and read into the adjacent gene and terminated at the PAS of the latter instead (Figure 9A–B and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by nanopore DRS data in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: The motif enriched at sites with differential error rate in T. gondii METTL3 KD is ARACW (R = A/G, W = A/T/G), which resembles the RGAC core motif established as the m6A consensus sequence.
source: We then analyzed the motifs around which the most significant peaks of error were mapped, which revealed a high and significant enrichment of a motif consisting of ARACW (R = A/G, W = A/T/G) (Figure 10B). This resembles the RGAC core motif which is the established m6A consensus sequence identified in P. falciparum (Baumgarten et al., 2019), A. thaliana (Parker et al., 2020), humans (Linder et al., 2015), and yeast (Schwartz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by motif analysis in Figure 10B.

claim: About 65% of the error sites mapped at the RRAC consensus motif in T. gondii.
source: About 65% of the error sites mapped at the RRAC consensus motif, which seems to be evolutionary conserved across canonical strains of T. gondii, as shown by the evaluation of individual methylation sites, suggesting that mRNA methylation is a cis-regulatory feature conserved at the gene level (Figure 10D–F and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figures 10D-F.

claim: Putative m6A sites are located mostly at 3'UTR in T. gondii.
source: This error-based identification of methylation sites enabled us to locate putative m6A sites mostly at 3'UTR (Figure 10C), but most importantly, at sites where the canonical proximal PAS is overrun, as seen in the context of the depletion of METTL3 and CPSF4 (Figure 10D–F, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B, Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Figure 8D, and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by metagene analysis in Figure 10C.

claim: Many loci with termination defects presented significant error peaks at the putative 3' termination site.
source: In fact, many loci with termination defects presented significant error peaks at the putative 3' termination site (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 10C.

claim: The genes targeted by the readthrough phenotype following the KD of CPSF4 and METTL3 were mostly initially repressed and represented developmentally regulated genes adjacent to expressed tachyzoite genes.
source: In fact, the genes two that were displaying now higher amounts of nanopore-reads in the context of KD of METTL3 and CPSF4, were mostly, if not all, initially repressed, and represented developmentally regulated genes, that happen to be adjacent to expressed tachyzoite genes. The mRNA analysis of the set of genes that were targeted by this readthrough phenotype, illustrated their developmentally regulated nature (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by expression analysis in Figure 11A.

claim: Many of the genes targeted by readthrough are recognized as targets of the MORC repressor complex and their expression is upregulated following the KD of MORC.
source: Interestingly, many of these genes are recognized as targets of the MORC repressor complex and their expression is seen to be upregulated following the KD of MORC (Figure 11A; Farhat et al., 2020).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Farhat et al., 2020 and supported by data in Figure 11A.

claim: The read-through phenotype occurs following the KD of both CPSF4 and METTL3, but not of MORC, which only resulted in a conventional promoter-dependent upregulation of the initially repressed genes.
source: However, a detailed look at the nanopore-derived reads in the contexts of KD of the latter, when compared with those of CPSF4 and METTL3, provided enough proof that the read-through phenotype occurs following the KD of both CPSF4 or METTL3, but not of MORC, which only resulted in a conventional promoter-dependent upregulation of the initially repressed genes (Figure 8D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B, Figure 11B–D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by comparative nanopore data in Figures 8D, 11B-D.

claim: The m6A-dependent polyadenylation of gene1 and the m6A independent polyadenylation of gene2 are at the core of an essential mechanism aiding in the tight transcriptional regulation of developmental stage-specific regulated genes in T. gondii.
source: The recurrence of the dual expression pattern between gene1 and gene2, the first being specific to tachyzoite, and the second being repressed and only expressed in stages other than tachyzoite, suggests that the respective m6A-dependent polyadenylation of gene1 and the m6A independent polyadenylation of gene2, at the core of an essential mechanism aiding in the tight transcriptional regulation of developmental stage-specific regulated genes in T. gondii.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as a conclusion drawn from the data.

claim: ROP35 displays tachyzoite-specific expression and occurs upstream of a repressed gene (TgME49_304730) whose expression is specific to late sexual, early oocyst stages.
source: An illustrative example of this observation can be that of ROP35 (Figure 11B–D), a rhoptry gene that displays a tachyzoites specific expression, and which occurs upstream of a repressed gene, namely TgME49_304730, the expression of which is known to be specific to the late sexual, early oocyst stages (EES5 and oocyst D0) (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by expression data in Figure 11A.

claim: The mRNA levels of ROP35 were unaltered following the KD of METTL3 or CPSF4.
source: The mRNA levels of ROP35 were unaltered following the KD of METTL3 or of CPSF4, based on both illumina-seq and nanopore-seq data.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 11B.

claim: The expression of TgME49_304730 was clearly induced following the KD of CPSF4.
source: However, the expression of the downstream TgME49_304730 was clearly induced following the KD of CPSF4, as illustrated by illumina-seq (Figure 11B, top).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 11B.

claim: The upregulation of TgME49_304730 following CPSF4 KD was caused by an overrun of the ROP35 PAS and readthrough breaching the transcriptional unit of the downstream gene.
source: The analysis of the reads generated at these loci provides the evidence for this upregulation to be caused by an overrun of the ROP35 PAS and the readthrough breaching the transcriptional unit of the downstream gene2 (TgME49_304730), as well as the polyadenylation machinery terminating by using this alternative PAS, which can now be referred to as an m6A-independent PAS, as evidenced by the earlier results and the error-based m6A site identification (Figure 11C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by nanopore DRS data in Figure 11C.

claim: T. gondii genome has retained the genes encoding for METTL3 and METTL14 which together form a core catalytic complex, as well as the regulatory subunit WTAP.
source: As with many Apicomplexa, the T. gondii genome has retained the genes encoding for METTL3 and METTL14 which together are known to form a core catalytic complex, noting also the conservation of the regulatory subunit WTAP (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Baumgarten et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Baumgarten et al., 2019.

claim: T. gondii METTL3 has an active catalytic site while TgMETTL14 displays a disrupted SAM-binding motif, suggesting catalytic inactivity.
source: Sequence analysis suggests that T. gondii METTL3 has an active catalytic site while TgMETTL14 displays a disrupted SAM-binding motif, suggesting catalytic inactivity shown in Wang et al., 2016a, which is in agreement with the current models of METTL14 serving as an RNA-binding platform activating allosterically the catalytically active METTL3 (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with citations to Wang et al., 2016a and Wang et al., 2016b.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis failed to detect in apicomplexan genomes the auxiliary proteins that are usually found in the identified human m6A writer complexes.
source: Using bioinformatic analysis, we failed to detect in apicomplexan genomes the auxiliary proteins that are usually found in the identified human complexes, and that are thought to aid the catalytic core components in the correct m6A deposition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Balacco and Soller, 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Balacco and Soller, 2019.

claim: Intense punctate foci of METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP were detected, similarly to their human counterparts which accumulate as condensates within nuclear speckles.
source: Intense punctate foci were detected, similarly to their human counterparts which were seen to accumulate as condensates within nuclear speckles (Ping et al., 2014), with these latter representing phase-separated membrane-less organelles enriched in pre-mRNA splicing factors.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Ping et al., 2014.

claim: Two new partners of the m6A writer complex were identified: TGME49_226660 and TGME49_275990, which were detected abundantly in WTAP eluates but also in less quantity in METTL3 and METTL14 pull-downs.
source: Interestingly, our experiments also reveal the existence of two new partners, the uncharacterized proteins TGME49_226660 and TGME49_275990, which were detected abundantly in WTAP eluates but also in less quantity in METTL3 and METTL14 pull-down (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2C.

claim: In human cells, the total m6A content in mRNAs fell by ~75% only after 96 hr following the triple knockdown of METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP.
source: Despite the fact that in human cells, the total m6A content in the mRNAs also fell by ∼75% only after 96 hr following the triple knockdown of METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP Ke et al., 2015; our observations are still indicative of a high level of stability of the m6A modification which is probably maintained throughout the life of an mRNA transcript.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Ke et al., 2015.

claim: A lack of m6A demethylases is recognized in the Apicomplexa phylum.
source: This, in addition to the fact that as opposed to higher eukaryotes, a lack of m6A demethylases is recognized in the phylum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Baumgarten et al., 2019) so that the dynamic changes of this mark would potentially be intimately linked to the activity of its corresponding writers, but also that of its YTH-domain-containing readers.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Baumgarten et al., 2019.

claim: The N-terminal zinc finger domains of CPSF4 show only partial conservation, suggesting that although their function in PAS motif binding is probably conserved, the recognized motif may have diverged.
source: First, the N-terminal zinc finger domains, essential units in the canonical PAS motif (AUAAA) interaction, show only a partial conservation, which leads us to speculate that although their function in PAS motif binding is probably conserved, the recognized motif may have diverged.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as a speculation based on sequence analysis.

claim: The presence of a potential secondary binding groove in T. gondii CPSF4-YTH implies possibly multiple binding modes which could depend on RNA secondary structures or on the binding context with the PAS.
source: Intriguingly, however, the presence of a potential secondary binding groove implies possibly multiple binding modes which could depend on RNA secondary structures or on the binding context with the PAS.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as an inference from the crystal structure.

claim: The YTH domain is separated from the zinc fingers by an extended region which is predicted as disordered.
source: The YTH domain is separated from the zinc fingers by an extended region which is predicted as disordered.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text based on structural prediction.

claim: Song et al., 2021 showed that the disordered region between the YTH domain and zinc fingers in Arabidopsis thaliana CPSF30-L was involved in promoting liquid-liquid phase separated organelles.
source: Recently, Song et al., 2021 also showed that this same disordered region was involved in promoting liquid-liquid phase separated organelles by the CPSF30-L of Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Song et al., 2021.

claim: In T. gondii, there exists an m6A-dependent polyadenylation through which the m6A site guides the polyadenylation machinery via the ability of the CPSF4 YTH to bind this modification.
source: In parallel to the orthodox 3'end processing mechanism which occurs independently of the m6A modification, we propose the existence in T. gondii of an m6A-dependent polyadenylation through which the m6A site would guide the polyadenylation machinery, via the ability of the CPSF4 YTH to bind this modification, thus allowing the recognition of the respective m6A-dependent polyadenylation site, and the proper termination at a relevant locus.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: The m6A dependent polyadenylation was detected mainly at the ends of a set of tachyzoite-specific genes that are highly expressed and are adjacent to developmental stage-specific repressed genes.
source: This m6A dependent polyadenylation was detected mainly at the ends of a set of tachyzoites-specific genes that are highly expressed and are adjacent to developmental stage-specific repressed genes (Farhat et al., 2020), hence at sites where a highly efficient barrier is needed to partition the distinct transcriptional signatures of these tandem genes, thus preventing any aberrant readthrough of the polymerase that is actively transcribing the upstream tachyzoite gene.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Farhat et al., 2020.

claim: The high rate of transcription witnessed in the tachyzoite stage dampens down in other stages, which might explain why the parasite has prioritized a large set of tachyzoite genes by this m6A related transcriptional barrier at their 3'ends.
source: The high rate of transcription that is witnessed in this stage, dampens down in the other stages, these later stages being either slow in their proliferation or even quiescent, which might explain why the parasite has prioritized a large set of tachyzoite genes by this m6A related transcriptional barrier at their 3'ends.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as an explanation for the observed phenomenon.

claim: Most of the m6A related enzymes and most of the 3'end processing factors were found to be less expressed in latent stages than they were in highly replicative ones.
source: Additionally, the fact that most of the m6A related enzymes and most of the 3'end processing factors, were found to be less expressed in latent stages than they were in highly replicative ones, agrees with the requirement of this mark at these stages in particular (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The m6A mark seems to have a relatively long half-life and a low level of dynamism in T. gondii.
source: Although this differential concentration might hint at some level of stage-specific upstream regulation for this mark, the fact that no m6A erasers have been detected in T. gondii and that the mark seems to have a relatively long half-life hints at a low level of dynamism for this mark.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as an inference from the data.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, many sequenced PAS were classified as being m6A-dependent, with the termination of the respective transcripts being dependent on the specific binding of this modification by the YTH within CPSF30L.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, many sequenced PAS were classified as being m6A-dependent, with the termination of the respective transcripts being dependent on the specific binding of this modification by the YTH within CPSF30L (Parker et al., 2020; Pontier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with citations to Parker et al., 2020 and Pontier et al., 2019.

claim: The m6A-assisted polyadenylation has been suggested to serve as one of the mechanisms for prevention of aberrant transcription at recently rearranged loci in plants.
source: The m6A-assisted polyadenylation has recently been suggested to serve as one of the mechanisms for prevention of aberrant transcription at recently rearranged loci (Pontier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Pontier et al., 2019.

claim: The evolutionary divergence between plants and T. gondii drove each of them to evolve the m6A-dependent barrier for their respective needs.
source: Despite the functional conservation of the architecture of CPSF4 between plants and T. gondii, the evolutionary divergence between these species and the different homeostatic requirements emanating from either a static but free life style, or a multi-host parasitic one, drove each of them to evolve this m6A-dependent barrier for their respective needs.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as an interpretation of the evolutionary significance.

claim: Nanopore DRS allowed the observation of genome assembly artefacts and mis-annotated or non-annotated loci in the genome of T. gondii.
source: In addition, employing the nanopore DRS allowed us to observe events which we could not have captured through illumina-seq. Apart from the genome assembly artefacts emanating from the inaccuracy of conventional techniques to read the repetitive elements which exist broadly in this genome, there seem to be a fairly large amount of loci that were mis-annotated or even non-annotated in the genome of T. gondii.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text based on nanopore DRS data.

claim: The m6A modification has been linked to the translational potential of transcripts as well as to their stability in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Also, this modification has been linked to the translational potential of transcripts as well as to their stability in other apicomplexan parasites, namely in Plasmodium falciparum (Baumgarten et al., 2019), which brings our attention to whether this m6A/polyadenylation coupling would also serve this parasite in its transcriptional partitioning, especially in view of the conservation of the special evolutionary feature of a YTH being carried within its CPSF4 homolog.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Baumgarten et al., 2019.

claim: All CPSF subunits probed (CPSF1, CPSF3, CPSF2, CPSF4, Symplekin, Fip1, WDR33, and PAP) displayed nuclear staining by immunofluorescence.
source: These latter proteins along with Symplekin, Fip1, WDR33 and the putative poly (A) polymerase (PAP) partner which we also probed, all displayed nuclear staining by immunofluorescence (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All CPSF subunits are essential for the survival of the parasite based on tachyzoite fitness assessment.
source: Other than all the identified CPSF subunits seemingly sharing a nuclear-based localization, their tachyzoite-based fitness assessment suggests that they are all essential for the survival of the parasite (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by fitness data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All CPSF subunits display consistent levels of expression in the tachyzoite stage and other actively proliferating stages, while showing markedly lower levels in latent stages (cyst and immature oocyst stages).
source: This goes in accordance with the consistent level of expression of all the subunits, in the tachyzoite stage and other actively proliferating stages, while plotting their average expression profiles revealed markedly levels in latent stages that is cyst and immature oocyst stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ZNF2 from metazoa and fungi is conserved with the ZNF1 from plants, chromerids and Apicomplexa, suggesting that the function of recognizing nucleotides A1 and A2 might be conserved.
source: A close-up view of the CCCH-type zinc fingers highlights conservation between the ZNF2 from metazoa and fungi and the ZNF1 from plants, chromerids and Apicomplexa (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the function acknowledged for the metazoan CPSF4 might be conserved in the aforementioned counterparts, that former being an ability to recognize nucleotides A1 and A2 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The ZNF3 from plants, chromerids and Apicomplexa is conserved with the ZNF5 from metazoa and fungi, a motif involved in Fip1 recruitment.
source: Similarly, the ZNF3 from plants, chromerids and Apicomplexa is conserved with the ZNF5 from metazoa and fungi, a motif involved in Fip1 recruitment (Hamilton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Hamilton et al., 2019.

claim: The PAP enzyme was not detected in CPSF1, Fip1, or CPSF4 immunoprecipitation data, except for very weak amounts in WDR33 interactome analysis.
source: None of these subunits immunoprecipitation data allowed the detection of the PAP protein, despite the fact that we managed to purify the PAP-FLAG protein separately, except for WDR33 interactome analysis in which only very weak amounts of PAP were detected (Figure 1B–C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The lack of PAP detection in most immunoprecipitations could be explained by highly transient binding or weaker interactions that were disrupted during stringent salt washing conditions (up to 500 mM KCl).
source: This could be explained either by a highly transient binding mode of PAP, or by its featuring of weaker interactions within the complex that could have been disrupted during the stringent salt washing conditions (up to 500 mM KCl) of the purification steps.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as a possible explanation for the observation.

claim: Apicomplexan and plant species have a high number of shared protein architectures, an evolutionary consequence of an early algae-related endosymbiotic event.
source: It is worth noting that apicomplexan and plant species have a high number of shared proteins architectures, an evolutionary consequence of an early algae-related endosymbiotic event.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as background knowledge.

claim: Plant-like Apetala-2 (AP2) factors have a high regulatory potential in apicomplexans.
source: An archetype are the plant-like Apetala-2 (AP2) factors, which have a high regulatory potential in apicomplexans (Jeninga et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Jeninga et al., 2019.

claim: In animals, mutants defective in components of the m6A pathway show opposing effects on the choice of alternative polyadenylation (APA) sites.
source: In animals, mutants defective in components of the m6A pathway show opposing effects on the choice of alternative polyadenylation (APA) sites (Kasowitz et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with citations to Kasowitz et al., 2018 and Yue et al., 2018.

claim: In plants, the adenosines of the consensus polyadenylation signals (PAS) motif consisting of AAUAAA could themselves be methylated, as indicated by nanopore-based analysis showing an enrichment of PAS motifs around m6A motifs.
source: It has been recently revealed in plants, that the adenosines of the consensus polyadenylation signals (PAS) motif consisting of AAUAAA, could themselves be methylated, as a nanopore-based analysis indicated an enrichment of PAS motifs around m6A motifs (Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Parker et al., 2020.

claim: A link between the presence of an m6A site and the overrun of the respective proximal PAS by the 3'end processing machinery was briefly implied in plants.
source: A link between the presence of an m6A site and the overrun of the respective proximal PAS by the 3'end processing machinery was briefly implied in plants (Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Parker et al., 2020.

claim: Chimeric mRNAs were generated in plants in the context of a deficiency in the CPSF30-YTH (CPSF30L) isoform, hinting at transcriptional readthrough events and the involvement of the YTH domain of CPSF30 in this process.
source: Moreover, the fact that chimeric mRNAs were generated in plants, in the context of a deficiency in the CPSF30-YTH (CPSF30L) isoform, hints at transcriptional readthrough events taking place, and at the involvement of the YTH domain of CPSF30 in this process (Pontier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with a citation to Pontier et al., 2019.

claim: The overall architecture of the CPSF complex in Apicomplexa is still debated.
source: The overall architecture of the CPSF complex in Apicomplexa is still debated; unlike animals, plants, and yeast, for which the polyadenylating complexes have been well characterized.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as background information.

claim: Apart from bioinformatics-based identification of some CPSF subunits, no direct biochemical evidence has yet been established to support the interaction of these proteins in-vivo in Apicomplexa prior to this study.
source: Apart from bioinformatics-based identification of some of the subunits (Ospina-Villa et al., 2020; Stevens et al., 2018), no direct biochemical evidence has yet been established to support the interaction of these proteins in-vivo.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with citations to Ospina-Villa et al., 2020 and Stevens et al., 2018.

claim: CPSF1 immunoprecipitation displayed the most discernible and intact CPSF complex when analyzed by band-specific mass spectrometry-based proteomics.
source: Among these, CPSF1, WDR33, and Fip1 provided the clearest FLAG-mediated immunoprecipitation data (Figure 1B–C, Supplementary file 1), with CPSF1 displaying the most discernible and intact complex, when analyzed by band-specific mass spectrometry-based proteomics (Figure 1B–C, Supplementary file 1), which demonstrated the highest levels of abundance of the putative candidates within the bands corresponding to their respective predicted molecular weights.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1B-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Two unknown proteins, TGME49_261960 (carrying an RNA recognition motif) and TGME49_254210 (carrying a C2H2 zinc finger domain), were detected in high quantity in CPSF1 immunoprecipitation and may constitute apicomplexan-specific subunits of the CSTF or CPSF complexes.
source: A relatively high quantity was detected of two as yet unknown proteins which may constitute apicomplexan-specific subunits of the CSTF or CPSF complexes, namely TGME49_261960 carrying an RNA recognition motif, and TGME49_254210 carrying a C2H2 zing finger domain.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: The mostly non-structured nature of the Fip1 protein could suggest some degradation events taking place to justify the relatively poor peptide representativity of this subunit in the CPSF1 immunoprecipitation profiling.
source: It is worth noting that the mostly non-structured nature of the Fip1 protein could suggest some degradation events taking place to justify the relatively poor peptide representativity of this subunit in the CPSF1 immunoprecipitation profiling (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text as a possible explanation for the observation.
